name: mac-robber
why: A forensic tool that builds MAC-time timelines from filesystems, a window into how investigators reconstruct what happened on a disk.

brief.what_it_is: mac-robber is a digital investigation tool that collects metadata from allocated files in a mounted file system. Its output feeds the mactime tool in The Sleuth Kit, which builds a timeline of file activity. It is written in C and is based on the Perl grave-robber tool from TCT. The homepage describes it as a basic tool that should compile on any UNIX system.
brief.why_it_exists: It is meant for incident response, either on a live system or on a dead system analysed in a lab. The author says it is useful for file systems that The Sleuth Kit does not support, such as an obscure UNIX file system mounted read-only on a trusted machine.
brief.how_it_works: It reads file metadata through the operating system, so the file system must already be mounted, unlike Sleuth Kit tools that parse the file system directly. Because of this, it cannot see deleted files or files hidden by rootkits. The homepage says it will modify access times on directories mounted with write permissions. Its output goes to mactime to produce the timeline.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers only a mac-robber 1.02 source code download, dated Feb 12, 2010. It mentions no hardware, accounts, runtimes, or configuration. Installation details beyond the Homebrew package were not on the page.
brief.standout: It works by reading the mounted file system through the OS rather than parsing it, which lets it handle file systems Sleuth Kit cannot read. It is small enough that the author suggests it can run on a trusted machine against a suspect, read-only mounted disk.
brief.status: quiet. The only dated item on the homepage is the 1.02 release on Feb 12, 2010, which also switched to the new mactime body format. The homepage shows no later release or update, and I did not check the repository or commit history.
brief.caveats: It cannot recover deleted files or see rootkit-hidden files, because it relies on the mounted file system view. Running it on a writable mount changes directory access times, so mount read-only when evidence matters. The homepage shows only a source tarball, not a binary, and the last release is from 2010. The homepage lists no license.
quotes: mac-robber is a digital investigation tool that collects data from allocated files in a mounted file system.
mac-robber requires that the file system be mounted by the operating system, unlike the tools in The Sleuth Kit that process the file system themselves.
mac-robber is very basic C and should compile on any UNIX system.
